sentences.nl: Maar… ik wil je graag uitnodigen.
sentences.en: But… I would like to invite you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But… I want you gladly invite.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Maar" is a conjunction meaning "but," often used to introduce a contrast or exception.  
• "Ik wil je graag uitnodigen" is a sentence structure where "wil" (want) is the modal verb, "je" (you) is the object, "graag" (gladly) adds politeness or enthusiasm, and "uitnodigen" (invite) is the main verb in infinitive form.  
• The verb "uitnodigen" takes a direct object, which is "je" in this sentence.  
• "Graag" is used to indicate a preference or willingness and often appears after the subject or object.

Extra phrases:  
• "Ik wil graag koffie drinken." (I want to drink coffee gladly.)  
• "Zij wil je graag helpen." (She wants to help you gladly.)  
• "Wij willen graag meedoen." (We want to participate gladly.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik wil graag met je praten." (I would like to talk with you.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, using "graag" can make requests or invitations sound more polite and enthusiastic, reflecting a friendly and warm approach in communication.

sentences.nl: Dus het lijkt me het beste wanneer we het morgen doen.
sentences.en: So it seems best to me if we do it tomorrow.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Thus it seems to me the best when we it tomorrow do.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus" (Thus) is a conjunction used to introduce a conclusion or result.  
• "Het lijkt me" (It seems to me) uses the verb "lijken" (to seem), followed by "me" (to me), indicating personal opinion or belief.  
• "Het beste" (the best) is a superlative expression.  
• "Wanneer" (when) introduces a subordinate clause.  
• "We het morgen doen" (we it tomorrow do) has the verb "doen" (to do) placed at the end, which is typical in subordinate clauses in Dutch.

Extra phrases:
- "Het lijkt me een goed idee." (It seems a good idea to me.)
- "Wanneer je tijd hebt, kunnen we praten." (When you have time, we can talk.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dus het lijkt me verstandig om nu te vertrekken." (Thus it seems wise to me to leave now.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of "het lijkt me" is common in Dutch to express personal opinions or suggestions in a polite manner, often used in both casual and formal contexts.

sentences.nl: Dat is goed.

sentences.en: Gianluca tells Marieke what time she should come.

sentences.nl: Hij is erg blij met zijn afspraakje.
sentences.en: He is very happy with his date.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He is very happy with his date.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hij is erg blij" uses the structure "subject + verb + adverb + adjective," which is common in Dutch.  
• "Met" is a preposition meaning "with," used to indicate association or involvement.  
• "Afspraakje" is a diminutive of "afspraak," meaning "appointment" or "date," often used informally.

Examples:  
• Zij is erg trots op haar werk. (She is very proud of her work.)  
• Wij zijn erg tevreden met het resultaat. (We are very satisfied with the result.)  
• Hij heeft een afspraakje met zijn dokter. (He has an appointment with his doctor.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij is erg enthousiast over haar nieuwe baan. (She is very enthusiastic about her new job.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, diminutives like "afspraakje" are often used to convey a sense of informality or endearment, especially in social contexts like dating.

sentences.nl: Maar ook Martin heeft plannen.
sentences.en: But Martin also has plans.

sentences.nl: Hij belt met Lars.
sentences.en: He is calling Lars.

sentences.nl: Hoi Martin, weet je al wanneer je nog eens komt? — Kom je misschien naar de barbecue van de laatste avond? — Eh…
sentences.en: Hi Martin, do you already know when you'll come again? — Are you maybe coming to the barbecue on the last evening? — Uh…

sentences.nl: Ik kom morgen.
sentences.en: I am coming tomorrow.

sentences.nl: Weet je waarom dat beter is? — Marieke wil de laatste avond waarschijnlijk, met de studenten zijn.
sentences.en: Do you know why that is better? — Marieke probably wants to be with the students on the last evening.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Do you know why that better is? — Marieke wants the last evening probably, with the students to be.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a question structure "Weet je waarom" (Do you know why) followed by an indirect question.  
• "Waarschijnlijk" (probably) is an adverb that modifies the verb phrase "met de studenten zijn" (to be with the students), and it is separated by a comma for emphasis.  
• "Wil" is the modal verb meaning "wants," which is often followed by an infinitive verb such as "zijn" (to be).

Examples:  
- "Weet je hoe laat het is?" (Do you know what time it is?)  
- "Hij wil morgen naar de stad gaan." (He wants to go to the city tomorrow.)  
- "Waarschijnlijk komt ze later." (She will probably come later.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Weet je waarom ze zo vroeg vertrekt? — Ze wil de trein niet missen. (Do you know why she leaves so early? — She doesn't want to miss the train.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• When discussing plans or preferences, Dutch people often use modals like "wil" to express desires or intentions clearly, reflecting their direct communication style.

sentences.nl: Dus morgen is de laatste kans, om samen naar het meertje te gaan.
sentences.en: So tomorrow is the last chance to go to the lake together.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So tomorrow is the last chance to together to the little lake to go.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus" is a conjunction meaning "so" or "therefore," often used to indicate a conclusion or consequence.  
• "Morgen" is an adverb meaning "tomorrow," indicating future tense.  
• "De laatste kans" translates to "the last chance," where "laatste" is the superlative form of "laat" (late).  
• "Samen" means "together," indicating joint action.  
• "Naar het meertje" means "to the little lake," where "meertje" is the diminutive form of "meer" (lake).  
• "Te gaan" is an infinitive construction, common in Dutch for indicating purpose or future action.

Extra Examples:  
• "Dus we moeten nu beslissen." (So we must decide now.)  
• "Morgen gaan we naar de markt." (Tomorrow we go to the market.)  
• "Dit is je laatste kans om het te doen." (This is your last chance to do it.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dus vanavond is de laatste mogelijkheid om het concert te zien." (So tonight is the last opportunity to see the concert.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No related culture notes.

sentences.nl: OK.
sentences.en: OK.

sentences.nl: Kun je zeggen hoe laat je hier bent? — Ik weet nog niet precies welke trein ik neem.
sentences.en: Can you say what time you'll be here? — I don't know exactly which train I'll take yet.

sentences.nl: Maar ik denk dat ik rond acht uur aankom.
sentences.en: But I think that I will arrive around eight o'clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But I think that I around eight o'clock arrive.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a subordinate clause introduced by "dat" (that), which pushes the verb "aankom" (arrive) to the end of the clause.  
• "Rond" (around) is used to indicate an approximate time.  
• "Denk" (think) is in the present tense and introduces an indirect statement.

• Example: "Ik weet dat hij morgen komt." (I know that he is coming tomorrow.)  
• Example: "Zij zegt dat ze het boek leest." (She says that she is reading the book.)  
• Example: "We komen rond half negen aan." (We arrive around half past eight.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maar ik verwacht dat ik rond zes uur vertrek." (But I expect that I leave around six o'clock.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, being punctual is generally considered important, although there is some flexibility with times indicated by "rond" (around).

sentences.nl: Kan ik bij jou op de kamer blijven slapen? — Dan neem ik mijn slaapzak mee.
sentences.en: Can I stay over in your room? — Then I'll bring my sleeping bag.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Can I at you in the room stay sleep? — Then take I my sleeping bag with.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Kan ik bij jou op de kamer blijven slapen?" uses modal verb "kan" (can) which requires the infinitive "slapen" (to sleep) at the end.  
• "Bij jou" means "at your place" or "with you," showing location or proximity.  
• "Dan neem ik mijn slaapzak mee" uses "dan" to indicate a consequence or plan, and "mee" (with) is a separable prefix verb construction with "neem" (take).

Examples:  
• "Kan ik bij je komen eten?" (Can I come to eat with you?)  
• "Blijf je bij ons slapen?" (Are you staying with us to sleep?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Mag ik bij jou op de bank zitten?" (May I sit on the couch with you?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Staying over at a friend's place is common in Dutch culture, especially among young people and students, often involving bringing a sleeping bag.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

waarom.spelling: The open syllable ‘wa-’ shows a long /aː/ sound, while ‘-rom’ has a short /ɔ/.
waarom.fast: In fast speech, the final /m/ in ‘waarom ik’ can assimilate with a following vowel, sometimes sounding like [ʋaːˈrɔmɪk].

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

weet.spelling: Open syllable we- indicates a long /eː/ sound.
weet.fast: In rapid speech, final /t/ in ‘weet ik’ may become a glottal stop [ʔ] before a vowel.

niet.spelling: The vowel 'ie' is pronounced as a long /iː/ sound.
niet.fast: In casual speech, the /t/ in 'niet' may become unreleased or assimilate to a following consonant.

hoe.spelling: The vowel sound /uː/ in 'hoe' is represented by the letters 'oe', a common Dutch spelling for this sound.
hoe.fast: In rapid speech, the /ˈɦuː/ in ‘hoe gaat’ may blend, with the /ɦ/ becoming less pronounced, sounding like /uːɣaːt/.

wil.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ in wil closes with the liquid /l/.
wil.fast: In fast speech, ‘wil ik’ may blend, reducing the /l/ to a lighter touch before the vowel.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

welke.spelling: The 'w' in Dutch is pronounced closer to an English 'v', while 'e' is short, creating /ɛ/.
welke.fast: The initial /ʋ/ in ‘welke’ may be pronounced as a [v] when followed by a vowel in fast speech.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
dan.fast: In rapid speech, 'dan ik' may have the /n/ assimilated to [ŋ] before a velar sound.

doen.spelling: The spelling ‘oe’ consistently represents the long /u/ sound.
doen.fast: In fast speech, final /n/ in ‘doen’ often becomes nasalized or drops before a vowel, as in ‘doe ik’.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

tot.spelling: The word 'tot' follows the closed syllable pattern, resulting in a short vowel sound /ɔ/.
tot.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'tot' may become less aspirated or even assimilate with a following consonant.

aflevering.spelling: The prefix ‘af-’ indicates a separable prefix, showing a clear boundary with the root.
aflevering.fast: The initial /f/ of ‘aflevering’ may assimilate to a voiced [v] in connected speech, especially after voiced sounds.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

zin.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in ‘zin heb’ may be realized as a nasalized vowel or dropped in informal contexts.
